title: Stored Functions, Return Types and Determinism
description: Design scalar stored functions with explicit return types, NULL policies, determinism and privilege contracts, then test boundary arithmetic and per-row execution costs.

questions.question_text: What does a SQL stored function return?
options: One value through its declared return type
An arbitrary number of independent result sets
questions.explanation: The function is used as a scalar routine in supported expressions.

questions.question_text: How does the shown stored function differ from a procedure?
options: It is called in an expression rather than invoked through CALL
It automatically owns the caller transaction
questions.explanation: Invocation and output contracts differ.

questions.question_text: What is billed_hours(61) under the stated rule?
questions.explanation: The positive duration crosses the second whole-hour boundary.

questions.question_text: What is billed_hours(0)?
questions.explanation: Zero is a known valid duration under this contract.

questions.question_text: What does the function return for a negative duration here?
questions.explanation: The explicit teaching policy rejects negative input through NULL.

questions.question_text: Does writing DETERMINISTIC prove every possible implementation behaves deterministically?
options: Yes, the server proves all behavior
questions.explanation: The declaration must truthfully describe the actual routine.

questions.question_text: What can make a function depend on more than its visible arguments?
options: A stable pure integer formula alone
questions.explanation: Environmental data can change between identical argument calls.

questions.question_text: What does NO SQL describe in the pure example?
options: A ban on calling the function from SQL
No SQL data access in the function body
questions.explanation: Routine data-access characteristics are distinct from invocation syntax.

questions.question_text: Why avoid adding 59 before dividing a very large minute input?
options: The addition can overflow a narrower integer range
questions.explanation: Algebraically similar formulas can have different finite-range behavior.

questions.question_text: Does a compact function call guarantee low per-row cost?
options: Yes, shorter text means faster execution
questions.explanation: Hidden lookups and outer population can dominate work.

questions.question_text: Can wrapping an indexed column in a function change access opportunities?
questions.explanation: The transformed predicate may not match an ordinary raw-column access path.

questions.question_text: Can a MySQL stored function independently COMMIT arbitrary caller work?
options: No, the context restricts transaction-control statements
questions.explanation: Stored functions are not general transaction-owning procedures.

questions.question_text: Can arbitrary result-set emission be treated as a scalar function contract?
options: Yes, all results become one value
questions.explanation: Use the appropriate routine type and supported statement context.

questions.question_text: Why test declared return type boundaries?
options: Correct mathematics can be narrowed or converted by the return representation
questions.explanation: Range, scale, length and collation can affect returned values.

questions.question_text: Can rounding each discounted line differ from rounding one combined total?
options: Only if all values are zero
questions.explanation: The rounding point is part of the business formula.

questions.question_text: Does an owner parameter prove caller authorization?
questions.explanation: Trusted identity and access enforcement are separate from the supplied value.

questions.question_text: What should a hosted routine-creation restriction trigger?
options: An exact capability report and reviewed resolution
questions.explanation: Creation restrictions are not permission to weaken the environment.

questions.question_text: Which inputs challenge the billed-hours boundaries?
questions.explanation: Missing, invalid, zero and exact boundaries test different branches.

questions.question_text: Does a MariaDB result establish exact MySQL provider behavior?
options: Only if the stored function is deterministic
questions.explanation: Compatibility and exact engine/provider evidence must remain separate.

questions.question_text: What does SQL SECURITY INVOKER specify?
options: Invoker privilege context under the engine contract
questions.explanation: Context still needs allowed and denied access tests.

coding_problems.title: Implement a pure billed-hours function
coding_problems.task: Create billed_hours(p_minutes INT) RETURNS INT as a DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL, SQL SECURITY INVOKER function. NULL or negative input returns NULL; zero returns zero; positive minutes round up to whole sixty-minute hours. Return duration_id and billed_hours for every supplied row, ordered by duration_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE durations(duration_id INT PRIMARY KEY,minutes INT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE FUNCTION billed_hours(p_minutes INT) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC NO SQL SQL SECURITY INVOKER RETURN CASE WHEN p_minutes IS NULL OR p_minutes<0 THEN NULL WHEN p_minutes=0 THEN 0 ELSE 1+((p_minutes-1) DIV 60) END; SELECT duration_id,billed_hours(minutes) AS billed_hours FROM durations ORDER BY duration_id;
hints: Use integer arithmetic with explicit invalid-input policy.
coding_problems.explanation: The positive formula adds one hour for any positive remainder while preserving zero and missingness rules.

coding_problems.title: Return a rounded ten-percent discount amount
coding_problems.task: Create discounted_amount(p_amount DECIMAL(10, 2)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10, 2) as a DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL, SQL SECURITY INVOKER function. NULL or negative input returns NULL; otherwise return ROUND(p_amount*0.90, 2). Return item_id and discounted_amount, ordered by item_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE fee_items(item_id INT PRIMARY KEY,amount DECIMAL(10,2) NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE FUNCTION discounted_amount(p_amount DECIMAL(10,2)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) DETERMINISTIC NO SQL SQL SECURITY INVOKER RETURN CASE WHEN p_amount IS NULL OR p_amount<0 THEN NULL ELSE ROUND(p_amount*0.90,2) END; SELECT item_id,discounted_amount(amount) AS discounted_amount FROM fee_items ORDER BY item_id;
hints: Keep the declared decimal representation and rounding explicit.
coding_problems.explanation: The exact decimal value 0.945 rounds to 0.95 under the stated rounding contract. Missing or negative inputs return NULL.

notes:
## Return one well-defined value from a stored routine

A stored function is a named database routine that returns one value through its declared return type. It can be called in supported SQL expressions, unlike a procedure invoked with CALL. A function is useful when one coherent calculation needs a reviewed reusable definition. It is not automatically preferable to a simple expression, and hiding a table lookup inside a function can make cost and access behavior harder for callers to see.

Consider converting workshop durations from minutes to billed hours under a precise rule: round each nonnegative duration up to a whole hour, keep zero as zero, and preserve a missing duration as NULL. The function's usefulness comes from this complete contract, not from having a short name. Negative durations need an explicit policy rather than being silently charged as if they were valid measurements.

## Define inputs, outputs and missingness together

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION billed_hours(p_minutes INT)
RETURNS INT
DETERMINISTIC
NO SQL
SQL SECURITY INVOKER
RETURN CASE WHEN p_minutes IS NULL OR p_minutes<0 THEN NULL
            WHEN p_minutes=0 THEN 0
            ELSE 1+((p_minutes-1) DIV 60) END;
```

For input 0 the result is 0; for 1 and 60 it is 1; for 61 it is 2. A negative input yields NULL under this teaching policy, and a NULL input stays NULL. The integer formula avoids relying on fractional division scale before rounding up. It also avoids adding 59 to a very large input, which could overflow a narrower integer domain. The input range and return capacity still require deliberate selection.

The declarations describe different aspects of the routine. RETURNS specifies the result type. DETERMINISTIC states an intended same-input/same-output property. NO SQL describes absence of SQL data access for this pure calculation. SQL SECURITY INVOKER declares execution context. None of these declarations replaces a test of the implementation's actual arithmetic, NULL policy or caller permissions.

## Distinguish deterministic logic from a declaration alone

A deterministic function returns the same result for the same arguments under its stated relevant environment. A clock-dependent function or one reading changing table contents has different behavior. Merely writing DETERMINISTIC does not make a changing calculation deterministic or prove that the server has exhaustively checked the assertion. Replication and binary-logging rules can make truthful routine characteristics operationally important.

A function that reads a current exchange rate from a table can change its result without changing its visible arguments. That may be a valid operation, but it is not the same contract as a pure conversion with an explicit rate argument. Make environmental dependencies visible in naming, parameters or documentation. Do not label a routine deterministic only to bypass creation restrictions or satisfy an expected checklist.

## Compare stored and built-in functions carefully

MySQL includes many built-in scalar functions for arithmetic, text and dates. A stored function can combine them into a domain calculation, but it also adds deployment, privilege and versioning responsibilities. A local expression can sometimes be clearer and easier to optimize. Choose reuse when it reduces ambiguity, not because every repeated three-token expression needs a new database object.

A stored function is distinct from a loadable native function or a client-language helper with a similar name. Creation syntax, privileges, execution environment and failure modes differ. Keep the lesson's scope on SQL stored functions and label vendor-specific features. A query running on MariaDB is compatibility evidence for that environment, not verification of every MySQL configuration or hosted execution provider.

## Keep table access and per-row cost visible

A function called in a SELECT list can be invoked across many candidate rows. If it performs a table lookup on every call, the workload can grow with the outer population even when the query text looks compact. Optimizer transformations and evaluation choices vary, so neither one physical call per displayed row nor automatic caching should be asserted without evidence. Measure the actual plan and representative execution.

Applying a function to an indexed column in a filter can change access opportunities. A predicate comparing a transformed value is not necessarily served by the ordinary raw-column index. A supported functional index or a rewrite preserving semantics can help in some engines, but these require their own restrictions and migration review. Do not make a function-based filter fast by weakening its NULL or comparison contract.

## Observe stored-function restrictions

MySQL stored functions cannot be used as general procedures that emit arbitrary result sets or independently control transactions. Statements that perform explicit or implicit commit or rollback are restricted in this context. Dynamic SQL facilities available in some procedure contexts are also restricted for stored functions. Read the actual server rules before moving an existing multi-statement procedure into a function body.

A function must not modify a table already being used by the invoking statement in ways forbidden by the engine. Hidden writes inside apparently scalar expressions can create surprising side effects and restrictions. Prefer a pure calculation for introductory functions, and make any approved data access explicit. A caller should not discover that displaying a label also changes operational records or opens an unexpected authority path.

## Review return types and conversion boundaries

The declared return type can constrain, round or convert a computed value. Test the exact boundary for integer range, decimal precision, text length and collation as relevant. A calculation producing a mathematically correct value can still return an incorrect stored representation if its type is too narrow. SQL modes can influence whether a conversion is rejected or reported differently, so record the environment when testing edge behavior.

For a decimal fee function, define the rate, rounding point and treatment of negative or missing amounts. Rounding every line and then summing can differ from summing exact lines and rounding once. The function's placement in a larger report therefore matters. A reusable calculation should state the unit and rounding contract so callers do not compose it into a different unintended formula.

## Keep privileges and definer context deliberate

Invoker execution uses the caller's relevant privilege context. Definer-context routines can exercise different capabilities and therefore require careful review of permitted inputs and resource scope. A function accepting an arbitrary owner identifier does not establish that the caller owns the referenced record. Binding values prevents code injection only when the execution design preserves that separation; it does not supply missing authorization.

Routine creation and execution can require privileges affected by server configuration and binary logging. A failure to create a function in a hosted environment does not justify turning off safety controls or requesting broader secrets. Report the exact unsupported capability or required reviewed operation. These lesson examples create no application functions and change no live grants; their execution belongs only in a disposable teaching environment.

## Test the function as a contract

Create a table of inputs and expected outputs before executing the function. For billed hours, test NULL, -1, 0, 1, 59, 60, 61 and a larger positive value. Check that the input row identity remains visible so two equal outputs are not confused with duplicate input removal. A result-level fixture establishes arithmetic for those cases, while privileges, concurrency and provider compatibility remain separate evidence.

For the second exercise, a pure discount calculation returns a two-decimal amount after a fixed ten-percent reduction. NULL or negative inputs return NULL under the defined policy. Test 0, 10 and a value whose reduced amount needs rounding. Explain why a numeric zero is a known valid amount while NULL represents missing or rejected input; do not replace them indiscriminately in a report.

## Solve two reuse decisions

First exercise: implement billed_hours with the stated integer rule and return its value for every supplied duration row. The worked answers are 0→0, 1→1, 60→1 and 61→2, with missing or negative inputs mapped to NULL. Compare the result with an unsafe formula that adds 59 before dividing and explain the potential range issue without claiming a measured failure on an untested provider.

Second exercise: implement the fixed discount calculation using a declared decimal return type and explicit rounding. Then compare a query using the function in its projection with one using it in a filter over many rows. The arithmetic contract is the same, but access paths and evaluation cost can differ. Continue with [numeric functions](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/numeric-functions), [stored procedure contracts](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/stored-procedure-contracts) and [function-based index concepts](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/function-based-index-concept) for the surrounding expression and execution boundaries.
